title: Local matrix models in the semisimple rank-one cases
statement: Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. An $S$-group scheme is a group object in schemes over $S$, with multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams of [def-sc-group-scheme] over this base. A reductive $S$-group means a smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] affine finite-type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] $S$-group all of whose geometric fibres are connected [def-weil-connected-scheme] and have no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup. Unipotent means that every geometric point is unipotent in a faithful matrix representation. A split maximal torus $T\hookrightarrow G$ is a closed subgroup [def-weil-closed-immersion] isomorphic to $\mathbf G_{m,S}^r$, $r\geq0$, maximal among tori on every geometric fibre; a torus over an algebraically closed field is a product of multiplicative groups. Here $\mathbf G_{m,S}=\operatorname{Spec}A[z,z^{-1}]$ with multiplication of units. Semisimple rank one means that the quotient of each geometric fibre by its largest smooth connected normal solvable subgroup has maximal tori of dimension one; solvable means that successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups become trivial. The centre is the subgroup functor of points commuting with every point after every algebra extension. Let $H$ be reductive of semisimple rank one with split maximal torus $T$. Suppose its centre is finite locally free of constant rank $d\in\{1,2\}$, meaning its coordinate module is locally free of rank $d$ over $\mathcal O_S$. If $d=1$, there is a Zariski open cover on which $(H,T)$ is isomorphic to $(\operatorname{PGL}_{2,S},D_{\mathrm{PGL}})$. If $d=2$, there is a Zariski open cover on which $(H,T)$ is isomorphic to $(\operatorname{SL}_{2,S},D_{\mathrm{SL}})$. The cover may be refined to affine opens. Here $\operatorname{SL}_2(R)$ consists of determinant-one matrices over each commutative $S$-algebra $R$; $\operatorname{PGL}_2$ is the fppf sheaf quotient of the group of invertible matrices $\operatorname{GL}_2$ by scalar invertible matrices, with fppf coverings meaning faithfully flat finitely presented coverings; $D_{\mathrm{SL}}$ is the determinant-one diagonal subgroup and $D_{\mathrm{PGL}}$ the image of the diagonal subgroup. The chosen isomorphisms remain isomorphisms after every base change. No residue characteristic is excluded.

source.place: Conrad, Proposition 4.2.7 and proof, printed pp.123--124 (trivial centre); Proposition 4.3.4 and proof, printed pp.131--132 (centre of order two). Read online; WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf. No Stacks tag states this relative structural theorem.

proof.text: Record the standard exact sequence of fppf group sheaves $1\to\mu_2\to\operatorname{SL}_2\xrightarrow{q_0}\operatorname{PGL}_2\to1$ by calculation. The projective-frame theorem gives local matrix lifts. For a lift $M\in\operatorname{GL}_2(R)$, put $\delta=\det M\in R^\times$ and pass to $R[t]/(t^2-\delta)$, free of rank two with $t$ invertible; $t^{-1}M$ has determinant one. This extension is faithfully flat and finitely presented, so gives the required fppf lift. A determinant-one matrix maps to the identity exactly when it is $uI$ with $u^2=1$. Also $q_0^{-1}(D_{\mathrm{PGL}})=D_{\mathrm{SL}}$: being projectively diagonal forces both off-diagonal entries to vanish after a faithfully flat scalar lift, hence already over the original ring. These descriptions hold on every test scheme by gluing affine tests.

source.place: Elementary matrix expansion of the standard central quotient used in Proposition 4.3.4, printed p.131; no division by two.

proof.text: First prove the case $d=1$. If $C$ is the coordinate algebra of the centre, its augmentation and unit split $C=A\oplus I$. Since $C$ is locally free of rank one, the direct summand $I$ has rank zero and is zero; thus $Z(H)=1_S$. Apply the relative adjoint flag-curve lemma to $(H,T)$, after its specified Zariski restriction. It supplies $T\subseteq B\subseteq H$, a smooth proper quotient $X=H/B$, the section $\sigma=1\bmod B$, and the geometric-fibre isomorphisms given by the translation action.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.7, proof, printed pp.123--124, through the section sigma.

proof.text: Apply the pointed-family lemma to $(X,\sigma)$ to arrange $X\simeq\mathbf P^1_S$ with $\sigma$ at infinity, on a further open cover. The base is still Noetherian. The projective-frame theorem with rank two identifies its automorphism sheaf with $\operatorname{PGL}_2$, so translation gives a group morphism $\phi:H\to\operatorname{PGL}_2$. On every geometric fibre this is an isomorphism by the flag-curve lemma. Both source and target are smooth over $S$; the map is locally finitely presented. Explicitly, on affine patches both coordinate algebras are finitely generated over a Noetherian base ring: generators for the source algebra over the base also generate over the target algebra, and the kernel of the resulting polynomial presentation is finitely generated. The geometric-fibre criterion now makes $\phi$ an isomorphism. Since $B$ fixes $\sigma$, $\phi(T)\subseteq B_\infty$, where fixing infinity is precisely the vanishing of the lower-left matrix entry on each local matrix lift.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.7, proof, printed p.124, action on the trivialized quotient and fibral isomorphism test.

proof.text: The image $\phi(T)$ is a maximal torus, since $\phi$ is a group isomorphism. Apply the triangular-torus lemma and postcompose $\phi$ with conjugation by its local section $b$. This carries $T$ to $D_{\mathrm{PGL}}$. Thus steps 2--4 have proved the entire trivial-centre assertion, including its specified torus, for any affine Noetherian base with these hypotheses.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.7, last paragraph of proof, printed p.124.

proof.text: Now let $d=2$. The relative centre theorem makes $Z=Z(H)$ a multiplicative-type closed subgroup with formation compatible with base change. Fppf locally it is $D(N)$; its coordinate algebra is free with basis $N$, so rank two forces $N\simeq\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z$. Consequently $Z$ is fppf locally $\mu_2$. The character-duality theorem says that $\operatorname{Aut}(\mu_2)=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z)=1$, also over nonreduced bases. The local identifications therefore agree on overlaps and glue to $Z\simeq\mu_2$. This uses the sheaf property of represented functors, rather than any assertion that geometric points determine arbitrary scheme maps.

source.place: Proposition 4.3.4, opening centre argument, printed p.131; Theorem 3.3.4 and Appendix B.1.

proof.text: The central-quotient theorem supplies a reductive $Q=H/Z$ with trivial centre, quotient maximal torus $\overline T=T/Z$, and $p^{-1}(\overline T)=T$. This torus is split Zariski locally: write $T=D(\mathbf Z^r)$; the inclusion $\mu_2\hookrightarrow T$ corresponds locally to a surjection $u:\mathbf Z^r\to\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z$, and duality gives $T/\mu_2=D(\ker u)$. If $u(e_j)=1$ and $u(e_i)=c_i\in\{0,1\}$, a basis of $\ker u$ is $2e_j$ together with $e_i-c_ie_j$ for $i\ne j$. On each geometric fibre the field classification shows that finite centre of order two forces $H_{\bar s}\simeq\operatorname{SL}_2$: the displayed central torus factors and the GL2 case have positive-dimensional centre, and PGL2 has trivial centre. By step 1 its central quotient is PGL2; hence $Q$ has semisimple rank one. Apply the already established steps 2--4 to $(Q,\overline T)$, refining by affine opens, to get $\theta:(Q,\overline T)\simeq(\operatorname{PGL}_2,D_{\mathrm{PGL}})$.

source.place: Proposition 4.3.4, first paragraph of proof, printed p.131; split-torus quotient basis written explicitly.

proof.text: Set $p'=\theta p$ and form the pullback group sheaf $E=H\times_{\operatorname{PGL}_2}\operatorname{SL}_2$ along $q_0$. Projection to the second factor gives $1\to Z\to E\to\operatorname{SL}_2\to1$, a central exact fppf extension: local lifts and its kernel are obtained by pulling back those of $p'$. Here $Z=\mu_2$ is a separated commutative group scheme, so Gabber's splitting theorem applies without a smoothness hypothesis on $Z$. Its splitting followed by projection to $H$ yields a homomorphism $f:\operatorname{SL}_2\to H$ with $p'f=q_0$. Thus $a=f|_{\mu_2}$ has values in $\ker p'=Z=\mu_2$.

source.place: Agent simplification of the central-extension argument of Proposition 4.3.4 using Proposition 4.3.1, printed pp.126--131.

proof.text: By character duality, locally on the base $a:\mu_2\to\mu_2$ is either the trivial homomorphism or the identity; the choice is locally constant. The trivial case is impossible. On any geometric fibre in that case, $f$ factors through the sheaf quotient $q_0$, giving a homomorphic section $s$ of $p'$. Then $(x,z)\mapsto s(x)z$ identifies $H_{\bar s}$ with $\operatorname{PGL}_{2,\bar s}\times\mu_{2,\bar s}$: the inverse sends $h$ to $(p'h,s(p'h)^{-1}h)$. In characteristic different from two the two values $1,-1$ disconnect this product; in characteristic two its coordinate rings contain the nonzero nilpotent $t-1$ with square zero, so it is not reduced, whereas a smooth geometric fibre is reduced. Both contradict the hypotheses on $H$. Thus $a$ is the identity everywhere, including over nilpotent bases.

source.place: Agent alternative to the pushout/kernel dichotomy in Proposition 4.3.4, printed pp.131--132; the scheme-theoretic order-two alternatives include characteristic two.

proof.text: The map $f$ is now an isomorphism of fppf sheaves. For injectivity, $f(g)=1$ implies $q_0(g)=1$, so $g\in\mu_2$, where $f$ is the identity onto $Z$. For surjectivity, given $h$, lift $p'h$ fppf locally to $g\in\operatorname{SL}_2$ by step 1; then $h f(g)^{-1}\in Z$, and multiplication of $g$ by the corresponding element of $\mu_2$ produces a preimage of $h$. Injectivity makes these local preimages agree, so they glue. Representability converts this sheaf isomorphism into a group-scheme isomorphism. Finally $p'^{-1}(D_{\mathrm{PGL}})=T$ by step 6 and $q_0^{-1}(D_{\mathrm{PGL}})=D_{\mathrm{SL}}$ by step 1. Since $p'f=q_0$, $f^{-1}(T)=D_{\mathrm{SL}}$, proving the torus clause.

source.place: Elementary assembly of the two central exact sequences and their kernel isomorphism; Proposition 4.3.4, torus correspondence paragraph, printed p.131.

proof.text: Refine the resulting open covers by affine opens. Restrict every chosen isomorphism and its inverse to these opens. For any subsequent base change, pull back both maps; their two composites remain the identity by functoriality of fibre products. The pulled-back subgroup identities are the same identities, so all chosen models preserve the named tori after every base change. None of the steps inverted two or any residue characteristic.

source.place: Elementary final restriction and base-change assembly of Propositions 4.2.7 and 4.3.4.
